Your 180 MB / ≈ 400 k‑polygon GeoJSON is far beyond what a browser can parse and render in a single request. The only practical fix is **stop feeding it to a `geojson` source** and turn it into a tiled data set (vector tiles, PMTiles, or raster tiles).
Below is a step‑by‑step “road‑map” you can follow right now, plus a few quick‑win tricks you can try while you’re converting the data.
## 1. Why GeoJSON fails at this size

column3: Why it happens
The whole file is fetched before any rendering can start.
Parsing a 180 MB string blocks the UI thread for seconds → “tab hangs”.
400 k polygons → millions of vertices → huge JavaScript objects → GC pressure → eventual crash.
Every polygon is drawn at every zoom, even when the map is zoomed out.

column1: Even if you minify or gzip the file, the browser still has to **download → decompress → parse → build a giant feature collection** before MapLibre can draw anything. That is why the tab sometimes dies.
## 2. Quick‑win “pre‑flight” optimisations (still not enough for 400 k polygons)

column3: How to do it
`mapshaper -i input.geojson -reduce-precision 5 -o out.geojson` (5‑digit decimal ≈ 1 m)
column4: Cuts size 30‑50 % without visible loss at typical web scales.

column3: `mapshaper -i input.geojson -simplify dp 10% keep-shapes -o out.geojson` (or use `topojson` to share vertices)
column4: Removes redundant vertices, reduces vertex count dramatically.

column3: Split the dataset into logical chunks (e.g. by admin level, by tile grid, by state) and serve each chunk as a separate GeoJSON URL.
column4: Allows you to load only the area the user is looking at (still heavy, but better).

column3: `new Worker('geojson-worker.js')` that does `self.onmessage = e => self.postMessage(JSON.parse(e.data))`
column4: Moves the parse cost off the UI thread, but you still end up with a 180 MB object in memory → not a long‑term solution.

column3: Ensure the HTTP response has `Content‑Encoding: gzip` (or `br`).
column4: Reduces network transfer, but parsing cost stays the same.

column1: > **Bottom line:** Even after all of the above you’ll still be loading a *single* 100‑150 MB JavaScript object into memory. That will never be smooth for a web map.

### 3.2. Turn your GeoJSON into vector tiles
#### Option A – **Tippecanoe** (fast, works on any OS)
# Install tippecanoe (brew, apt, or from source)
# Reduce precision & simplify on‑the‑fly (you can also pre‑process with mapshaper)

column3: Why it matters
Limit the zoom range you actually need (e.g. you never show parcels at zoom 0‑4).
Tippecanoe will automatically drop the most detailed features when a tile would exceed the size limit (default 500 KB).
Keeps full detail at high zooms, simplifies aggressively at low zooms.
Turn off hard caps if you want to control them yourself (but keep an eye on tile size).

column1: Result: `parcels.mbtiles` (SQLite‑based MBTiles) containing vector tiles for every zoom level you asked for.
#### Option B – **Planetiler** (Java‑based, great for huge OSM extracts)

If you already have an OSM‑derived extract or want to generate tiles from a PostGIS database, Planetiler can stream directly from the DB and produce **MLT** (MapLibre Tile) or **MVT** files. The workflow is similar to Tippecanoe but works better for > 10 M features.
# Convert the MBTiles produced by tippecanoe to PMTiles
Now you have a **180 MB → ~30 MB** (often 5‑10× smaller) archive that can be served from any static CDN.

column3: How to do it

column2: **Static CDN (S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, Netlify)**
column3: Upload the `.pmtiles` file, enable CORS (`*` or your domain).
column4: Free tier → a few dollars/month for > 10 TB egress.

column3: Deploy a Docker container or a small VM, point it at the MBTiles/PMTiles file.
Upload your MBTiles/PMTiles via their UI, get a style URL.
column4: Pay‑as‑you‑go, often $10‑30 / month for a few hundred GB.

column1: > **CORS is mandatory** – if you host the file on a different origin than your page, the server must send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). Most CDNs let you set this in the bucket policy.

### 4.2. Using a **standard vector source** (MBTiles via a tile server)
*If you run Martin:* `http://localhost:3000/tiles/parcels.json` will be auto‑generated.
### 4.3. Adding interactivity (click to get parcel ID)
Because the data is now **tiled**, only the tiles intersecting the current viewport are fetched, parsed, and kept in memory – a few hundred kilobytes at most, even at the highest zoom.
## 5. Optional: If you *must* keep a GeoJSON layer (e.g. for editing)

column3: How it helps

column2: **Chunked loading** (load one tile‑grid cell at a time)
column3: Reduces memory per request.
column4: Split the original GeoJSON into a folder structure like `z/x/y.geojson` (you can reuse the same tile grid you used for vector tiles). Load the appropriate file on `moveend` and add it as a temporary `geojson` source.

column3: `geojson-vt` creates client‑side vector tiles from raw GeoJSON on the fly, keeping the data in a worker thread.
Show only a simplified subset (e.g., centroids) when zoomed out.
column4: Use `filter` expressions in the style: `""filter"": ["">"", [""zoom""], 12]` to hide the layer at low zooms, or generate a separate “overview” layer with simplified geometries.

column1: These tricks can be useful for **editing** workflows where you need the full geometry client‑side, but they are **not a replacement** for proper tiling in a production viewer.

7. **Test**: open the map, open DevTools → Network → check that only a handful of `.pbf` (or `.pmtiles` range) requests are made when you pan/zoom.
